## What this exercise is

Exercises 4 and 5 asked whether counties with similar SMRs sit next to each
other. The **spatial scan statistic** asks a different question: *is there a
group of neighbouring counties where more people died than expected?* You can answer this question using **SaTScan**, on the same data: 2020 COVID-19 deaths in Pennsylvania's
67 counties.

Every SaTScan analysis rests on choices made before the scan runs. You make
three of them here and see how each changes the answer:

1. the **probability model** (Part B);
2. the **maximum size of the scanning window** (Part C);
3. how to read the **Monte Carlo $p$-value** (Part D).

**Everything runs from this file.** R writes SaTScan's input files and a
parameter file, runs SaTScan in the background, and reads the results back.
You do not need to open the SaTScan window. **All the R code is provided**;
you do not need to write new code. Run the chunks one at a time with the green
▶ button, read the output, and type your answer under each question. One or
two sentences per question is enough.

::: {.callout-important}

1. Install **SaTScan** (free) from [satscan.org](https://www.satscan.org),
   version 10.3 or later; the download asks you to fill in a short form.
   Keep the default location: on Windows the installer puts it in
   `C:\Program Files\SaTScan`; on a Mac, drag **SaTScan** into

## Part A --- Find SaTScan and prepare the input files (1.5 points)

This chunk repeats the first steps of Exercises 4 and 5: the join, the state
rate and the expected deaths.

```{r}
#| label: setup

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(rsatscan)                   # runs SaTScan from R
library(tigris)
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)

covid <- read_csv("data/pa_covid_deaths_2020.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(GEOID = sprintf("%05d", as.integer(FIPS)))      # text key, as in Ex. 4
pa <- counties(state = "PA", cb = TRUE, year = 2020, progress_bar = FALSE)

pa_covid <- pa |>
  left_join(covid, by = "GEOID") |>
  st_transform(5070) |>
  arrange(GEOID)

r <- sum(pa_covid$deaths_2020) / sum(pa_covid$Population)   # state rate
pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(E   = r * Population,                              # expected deaths
         SMR = deaths_2020 / E)
```

R needs to know where SaTScan's **batch program** is: the part of SaTScan that
runs without a window. The chunk looks in the places the installer uses.

```{r}
#| label: find-satscan

# if SaTScan is installed elsewhere, paste the full path to
# SaTScanBatch64.exe (Windows) or satscan (Mac) between the quotes
my_path <- ""

candidates <- c(my_path,
                "C:/Program Files/SaTScan/SaTScanBatch64.exe",      # Windows
                "C:/Program Files (x86)/SaTScan/SaTScanBatch.exe",  # Windows, 32-bit
                "/Applications/SaTScan.app/Contents/app/satscan",   # Mac
                "/opt/satscan/lib/app/satscan64")                   # Linux
ss_exe <- candidates[candidates != "" & file.exists(candidates)][1]
if (is.na(ss_exe)) stop("SaTScan not found: install it, or set my_path above")

ss_dir   <- dirname(ss_exe)                                 # its folder
ss_batch <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(ss_exe))     # its name
ss_exe
```

SaTScan reads three plain text files linked by a **location ID**, here the
county `GEOID`, exactly as in the lecture.

| File | Columns | Here |
|---|---|---|
| Case file `.cas` | location ID, number of cases | GEOID, deaths in 2020 |
| Population file `.pop` | location ID, year, population | GEOID, 2020, population |
| Coordinates file `.geo` | location ID, latitude, longitude | GEOID, county centroid |

```{r}
#| label: write-files

dir.create("satscan", showWarnings = FALSE)                  # folder for SaTScan
ss_folder <- normalizePath("satscan", winslash = "/")        # its full path

# county centroids in latitude / longitude
ll <- pa_covid |>
  st_centroid() |>
  st_transform(4326) |>                         # SaTScan wants lat/long
  st_coordinates()

# one plain table with everything SaTScan needs
ss <- pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(year = 2020,
         lat  = round(ll[, "Y"], 5),
         lon  = round(ll[, "X"], 5))

# three files, no header (rsatscan adds the extensions)
write.cas(select(ss, GEOID, deaths_2020),      ss_folder, "pa_covid")
write.pop(select(ss, GEOID, year, Population), ss_folder, "pa_covid")
write.geo(select(ss, GEOID, lat, lon),         ss_folder, "pa_covid")

# first three lines of each file
readLines("satscan/pa_covid.cas", n = 3)
readLines("satscan/pa_covid.pop", n = 3)
readLines("satscan/pa_covid.geo", n = 3)

# totals written to the files
c(deaths = sum(ss$deaths_2020), population = sum(ss$Population))
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Two common mistakes
- The coordinates file lists **latitude, then longitude**. Swapped, they put
  Pennsylvania in Antarctica, and SaTScan still runs.
- The location IDs must be **identical** in all three files. A county whose ID
  does not match is dropped without an error message.
:::

**A1.** How many deaths and how many people did you write to the files?

**There are 16,030 deaths and a population of 12,801,989.**

**A2.** SaTScan places each county at a single point, its centroid, and a
county enters a scanning circle when that point does. Think of a large rural
county whose people live mostly in one town near its edge. Why might the
centroid misplace that county's deaths?

**It would move the location of deaths to the center of the county instead of the edge of the county where they actually occur. Because the deaths are moved to the center of the county, it could not identify clusters accurately because the deaths would not be seen until the center of the county in SaTScan.**

## Part B --- Choose the model and run the scan (4.5 points)

### Which probability model?

SaTScan offers several probability models. The model depends on the **data
you have**, not on the result you hope for.

| Model | Data needed | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Poisson | case counts and population at risk | rates by area |
| Bernoulli | cases and controls (0/1 for each person) | case--control studies |
| Space--time permutation | case counts with dates, no population | rapid outbreak detection |
| Normal | a continuous measurement | e.g. birth weight, exposure levels |

**B1.** For each study, name the model you would choose and say in a few
words why. Copy the table and fill it in.

| Study | Model | Why |
|---|---|---|
| (a) COVID-19 deaths by county, with each county's population (this exercise) | **Poisson** | **Looking at the counts of COVID-19 deaths by counties in Pennsylvania.** |
| (b) Children born with a heart defect, and a random sample of children born without one, each with a home address | **Bernoulli** | **Having a case and control group, the study looking at children with heart defects and those without where the outcome is binary.** |
| (c) Daily emergency-room visits for diarrhoea by ZIP code, with no reliable population for the ZIP codes | **Space-time permutation** | **Getting the number of cases - emergency room visits for diarrhea, but no population, or no reliable population for zip codes** |
| (d) Blood lead level (µg/dL) of every child tested in each census tract | **Normal** | **Blood lead levels are a continuous measurement, and it's of all children in each census tract** |


**B2.** We scan **deaths**, yet the Poisson model also needs a **population**
file. What does SaTScan use the population for, and what is the null
hypothesis the scan tests?

**SaTScan uses the population for the LLR. The null hypothesis is that the ratio of the count of deaths and expected deaths is the same in all counties.**

### The settings

In class you chose the settings on the tabs of the SaTScan window. Here the
same settings go into a **parameter file** (`.prm`) that SaTScan reads. The
function below writes that file with `ss.options()` and then runs SaTScan.

| Setting in the code | Tab in the SaTScan window | Value here |
|---|---|---|
| `CaseFile`, `PopulationFile`, `CoordinatesFile` | Input | the three files from Part A |
| `CoordinatesType = 1` | Input | latitude / longitude |
| `PrecisionCaseTimes = 0` | Input | time precision: none |
| `AnalysisType = 1` | Analysis | purely spatial |
| `ModelType = 0` | Analysis | discrete Poisson |
| `ScanAreas` | Analysis | 1 = high rates, 2 = low rates |
| `MaxSpatialSizeInPopulationAtRisk` | Analysis → Advanced → Spatial Window | maximum window, % of population |
| `MonteCarloReps` | Analysis → Advanced → Inference | number of replications |
| `PValueReportType = 1` | Analysis → Advanced → Inference | standard Monte Carlo $p$-value |

Only three settings change between runs, so they are the function's
arguments: what to scan for, the maximum window and the number of
replications.

```{r}
#| label: run-satscan-function

run_satscan <- function(name, scan_for = "high", max_window = 50, reps = 999) {
  invisible(ss.options(reset = TRUE))                    # start from defaults
  ss.options(list(
    CaseFile           = "pa_covid.cas",                 # input files
    PopulationFile     = "pa_covid.pop",
    CoordinatesFile    = "pa_covid.geo",
    CoordinatesType    = 1,                              # latitude / longitude
    PrecisionCaseTimes = 0,                              # no dates
    StartDate          = "2020/1/1",
    EndDate            = "2020/12/31",
    AnalysisType       = 1,                              # purely spatial
    ModelType          = 0,                              # discrete Poisson
    ScanAreas          = if (scan_for == "high") 1 else 2,  # high or low rates
    MaxSpatialSizeInPopulationAtRisk = max_window,       # % of population
    SpatialWindowShapeType = 0,                          # circles
    MonteCarloReps     = reps,                           # random maps
    PValueReportType   = 1,                              # standard Monte Carlo
    SaveSimLLRsDBase   = "y",                            # keep their LLRs
    OutputGoogleMaps   = "n",                            # no extra output
    LaunchMapViewer    = "n",
    OutputShapefiles   = "n"))
  write.ss.prm(ss_folder, name)                          # parameter file
  res <- satscan(ss_folder, name, sslocation = ss_dir,
                 ssbatchfilename = ss_batch, cleanup = FALSE)   # run SaTScan
  if (!is.data.frame(res$col)) stop("SaTScan produced no clusters: check the files in Part A")
  res
}
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Why standard Monte Carlo?
SaTScan's default $p$-value replaces very small Monte Carlo $p$-values with an
approximation (Gumbel) and can print values such as $10^{-17}$. We ask for the
**standard Monte Carlo** $p$-value so that every $p$-value comes straight from
the replications, and you can check it by hand in Part D.
:::

### Run 1: `high50`

```{r}
#| label: run-high50

high50 <- run_satscan("high50", scan_for = "high", max_window = 50, reps = 999)
```

SaTScan wrote `high50.prm` (the settings), `high50.txt` (the results, for
people) and three `.dbf` files (the results, for software) in your `satscan`
folder. If you like, open `high50.prm` in the SaTScan window: the same
settings appear on the tabs you saw in class.

### Read the results

The top of `high50.txt` gives the SaTScan version, the analysis, and a
*SUMMARY OF DATA* that reports what SaTScan read:

```{r}
#| label: summary-of-data

txt   <- high50$main                                        # high50.txt, line by line
start <- grep("SUMMARY OF DATA", txt)
cat(txt[1:(start + 8)], sep = "\n")
```

Two helper functions turn the results into a table, with one row per cluster,
and a map. You do not need to understand them to use them.

```{r}
#| label: helpers
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Code for the two helper functions (optional)"

# table: one row per cluster SaTScan reported
ss_table <- function(res) {
  col <- res$col                                            # clusters
  gis <- res$gis                                            # counties in them
  out <- NULL
  for (k in col$CLUSTER) {
    cl     <- col[col$CLUSTER == k, ]                       # cluster k
    inside <- pa_covid$GEOID %in% trimws(as.character(gis$LOC_ID[gis$CLUSTER == k]))
    row <- data.frame(
      cluster   = k,
      counties  = paste(sort(pa_covid$NAME[inside]), collapse = ", "),
      n         = sum(inside),                              # number of counties
      pop_pct   = round(100 * sum(pa_covid$Population[inside]) /
                          sum(pa_covid$Population), 1),     # % of state population
      radius_km = round(cl$RADIUS),
      observed  = cl$OBSERVED,
      expected  = round(cl$EXPECTED),
      O_E       = round(cl$ODE, 2),                         # inside vs state rate
      RR        = round(cl$REL_RISK, 2),                    # inside vs outside
      LLR       = round(cl$LLR, 2),
      p_value   = cl$P_VALUE)
    out <- rbind(out, row)                                  # add the row
  }
  out
}

# map: clusters with p < 0.05 in colour (dark = most likely), the rest grey
ss_map <- function(res, title, colours = c("#67000D", "#CB181D", "#FB6A4A", "#FCBBA1")) {
  tab <- ss_table(res)
  gis <- res$gis
  sig <- tab$cluster[tab$p_value < 0.05]                    # significant clusters
  pa_covid$cluster <- NA                                    # no cluster yet
  for (k in sig) {
    ids <- trimws(as.character(gis$LOC_ID[gis$CLUSTER == k]))
    pa_covid$cluster[pa_covid$GEOID %in% ids] <- k
  }
  ggplot() +
    geom_sf(data = pa_covid, fill = "grey92", colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
    geom_sf(data = filter(pa_covid, !is.na(cluster)),
            aes(fill = factor(cluster)), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = colorRampPalette(colours)(length(sig)),
                      name = "Cluster") +                   # dark to light
    labs(title = title, subtitle = "Clusters with p < 0.05") +
    theme_void()
}
```

```{r}
#| label: results-50
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.5

tab50 <- ss_table(high50)
knitr::kable(tab50)                           # every cluster SaTScan reported

# the SMR map, for comparison, with the classes of Exercise 4
pa_covid <- pa_covid |>
  mutate(smr_class = cut(SMR, breaks = c(0, 0.5, 2/3, 0.9, 1/0.9, 1.5, 2, Inf),
                         labels = c("< 0.50", "0.50-0.67", "0.67-0.90", "0.90-1.11",
                                    "1.11-1.50", "1.50-2.00", "> 2.00")))
p_smr <- ggplot(pa_covid) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = smr_class), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdBu", direction = -1, drop = FALSE, name = "SMR") +
  labs(title = "SMR, 2020") +
  theme_void()

p_smr + ss_map(high50, "High-rate clusters, max 50%")
```

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `observed`, `expected` | deaths inside the circle, and the number expected at the state rate |
| `O_E` | observed / expected: the rate inside compared with the **state** rate |
| `RR` | relative risk: the rate inside divided by the rate **outside** the circle |
| `LLR` | log-likelihood ratio: the strength of the evidence; the largest is the most likely cluster |
| `radius_km` | distance from the circle's centre to its farthest county centroid |

**B3.** Compare the *SUMMARY OF DATA* printed above with your totals in A1.
Did SaTScan read every county, every death and every person? Why is this
check worth making before you read any cluster?
**SaTScan did read every county, death, and person. It’s important to check to confirm everything is there and correct because anything missing could affect the SaTScan clusters.**


**B4.** Describe the **most likely cluster** (cluster 1): how many counties,
what share of the state's population, its observed/expected ratio and its
relative risk. Look at the SMR map: is every county inside it above 1? Why is
its RR larger than its O/E?
**Cluster 1 has 22 counties, population of 6023384 which is 47% of the state’s population. The observed/expected ratio is 1.16 and relative risk is 1.34. In the SMR map, not every county in the most likely cluster has an SMR above 1. The RR is larger than OE because OE looks at the county vs the state rate and RR looks at the county vs area right outside of it.**



**B5.** How many clusters did SaTScan report, and how many have
$p < 0.05$? Why does SaTScan list clusters that are not significant, and why
does our map colour only those with $p < 0.05$?

**There were four clusters that SaTScan reported, and 3 had a p-value less than 0.05. The map only shows p<0.05 because 'sig' selects for only clusters <0.05. The line 'for (k in sig)' gives cluster numbers to only significant clusters. So when the ss_map using ggplot, colors are only assigned to significant clusters.**

## Part C --- The maximum window (4 points)

The 50% maximum is SaTScan's default, not a rule. We run the scan twice more,
changing **only** the maximum window.

```{r}
#| label: windows
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 3.5

high25 <- run_satscan("high25", scan_for = "high", max_window = 25, reps = 999)
high15 <- run_satscan("high15", scan_for = "high", max_window = 15, reps = 999)

tab25 <- ss_table(high25)
tab15 <- ss_table(high15)

knitr::kable(tab25, caption = "Maximum 25%")
knitr::kable(tab15, caption = "Maximum 15%")

# the three runs side by side
ss_map(high50, "Max 50%") + ss_map(high25, "Max 25%") + ss_map(high15, "Max 15%")

# one line per run, for the most likely cluster
runs <- list("50%" = tab50, "25%" = tab25, "15%" = tab15)
compare <- NULL
for (w in names(runs)) {
  tab <- runs[[w]]
  compare <- rbind(compare, data.frame(
    max_window   = w,
    significant  = sum(tab$p_value < 0.05),     # clusters with p < 0.05
    mlc_counties = tab$n[1],                    # most likely cluster
    mlc_pop_pct  = tab$pop_pct[1],
    mlc_RR       = tab$RR[1],
    mlc_LLR      = tab$LLR[1]))
}
knitr::kable(compare)
```

**C1.** How does the most likely cluster change from the 50% to the 25% to the
15% window? Name its counties in the 15% run.
**Everything decreases except the number of significant clusters increase. In the 15%, there is only 1 county, compared to the 21 counties with 50%.**


**C2.** Which clusters appear in all three runs, with the same counties? Why
does a cluster that survives a change of window deserve more confidence than
one that does not?

**The clusters that appear in all three runs: Bedford, Blair, Cambria, Indiana; Beaver, Lawrence; Huntingdon, Juniata, Mifflin. If the clusters remain the same then their clustering isn't dependent on the window size, but this doesn't mean that the results are statistically significant.**

**C3.** The window is defined by **population**, not by distance. Use the
`radius_km` column to compare a cluster in the Philadelphia area with one in
central or western Pennsylvania. Why are the circles so different in size?
In the 15% run, could Philadelphia and Delaware counties ever fall in the same
cluster? (Hint: `pop_pct`.)

**Since the county appears as a centroid, counties that have the maximum window as their population size would show 0 km, whereas multiple counties take up more space and have larger radii. In the 15% run, because of their population sizes, Philadelphia and Delaware counties could not fall into the same cluster.**


**C4.** Which maximum window would you use in a report to the Pennsylvania
Department of Health, and why? There is no single right answer; give a
reason.

**I would use 15% because it identifies smaller clusters that would be easier to target public health interventions or outreach programs. It's also useful for prioritizing areas of higher risk by looking at the highest clusters.**

## Part D --- The Monte Carlo $p$-value (4.5 points)

SaTScan redistributes the observed deaths at random among the counties, in
proportion to their expected deaths, scans that random map with every circle,
and keeps the **largest** LLR. It repeats this 999 times, and our settings
asked it to save those 999 values (`high50.llr.dbf`). In the histogram, the
dashed line marks their 95th percentile: the LLR a cluster needs for
$p < 0.05$.

```{r}
#| label: monte-carlo
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.5

sims  <- high50$llr$LLR                    # largest LLR of each random map
col50 <- high50$col                        # the clusters, unrounded
length(sims)

ggplot(data.frame(LLR = sims), aes(x = LLR)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey75", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = col50$LLR, colour = "red") +                  # our clusters
  geom_vline(xintercept = quantile(sims, 0.95), linetype = "dashed") +  # p = 0.05
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = "Largest LLR in each random map (grey) and in our clusters (red)",
       x = "LLR (log scale)", y = "Random maps") +
  theme_minimal()

# the p-value by hand, for each cluster
p_hand <- numeric(nrow(col50))
for (k in 1:nrow(col50)) {
  beat      <- sum(sims >= col50$LLR[k])            # random maps at least as high
  p_hand[k] <- (beat + 1) / (length(sims) + 1)
}
knitr::kable(data.frame(cluster   = col50$CLUSTER,
                        LLR       = round(col50$LLR, 2),
                        p_satscan = col50$P_VALUE,
                        p_by_hand = p_hand))
```

**D1.** In your own words, what does one grey value in the histogram
represent? Why is it the **largest** LLR of each random map that is kept,
rather than the LLR of one circle?
**One gray value in the histogram represents the largest LLR in a map simulation. It keeps the largest LLR from each simulation because it scans many circles to identify the most likely cluster. Using the largest LLR allows for comparison between observed clusters to the strongest clusters that can occur by change.**

**D2.** Do your hand-computed $p$-values match SaTScan's? Explain the formula
in words. What is the smallest $p$-value 999 replications can give?
**They do match SaTScan's values because they use the same Monte Carlo simulations. The p-value is calculated by counting how many random maps have a maximum LLR greater than or equal to the observed cluster's LLR, add 1, and dividing by the total number of simulations plus 1. With 999 simulations, the smallest possible p-value is 0.001.**


Now the same scan as `high25`, but with only **99** replications.

```{r}
#| label: replications

high25_r99 <- run_satscan("high25_r99", scan_for = "high", max_window = 25, reps = 99)
tab25_99   <- ss_table(high25_r99)

# same clusters, two numbers of replications
left_join(select(tab25,    cluster, counties, LLR, p_999 = p_value),
          select(tab25_99, counties, p_99 = p_value),
          by = "counties") |>
  knitr::kable()
```

**D3.** The clusters and their LLRs are the same in both runs; only the
$p$-values change. What is the smallest $p$-value with 99 replications?
Compare the $p$-values of the most likely cluster and of the weakest cluster
in the two runs. Why do analysts use 999 or 9,999 replications rather than 99?

**The smallest p-value with 99 replications is 0.01 but 0.001 for 999. For the weakest cluster, the p-value is 0.046 for 999 and 0.07 for 99. Running 999 or 9,999 replications can reduce the variation in p-value estimates and give more precise p-values.**

**D4.** SaTScan looked at thousands of circles, yet we apply no
multiple-testing correction. Local Moran's I, by contrast, runs one test per
county and needs one. Why is the scan's $p$-value already protected against
having searched so many circles?

**For SaTScan, it uses Monte Carlo simulation and only keeps the largest LLR, so the clusters are compared to the most likely cluster of all the circles rather than just one. But Local Moran's I tests each county separately.**

**D5.** A classmate writes: "The most likely cluster has $p = 0.001$, so there
is a 99.9% chance that it is a real cluster." Is this right? Rewrite the
sentence so that it is correct.

**There is a 0.1% chance of finding a cluster with an LLR as large or larger than the observed cluster's LLR.**

---

## Part E --- Scanning for low rates (2 points)

The scan can also look for areas with **fewer** deaths than expected. One more
run, with the 25% window and 999 replications.

```{r}
#| label: low-rates
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.5

low25 <- run_satscan("low25", scan_for = "low", max_window = 25, reps = 999)
knitr::kable(ss_table(low25))

ss_map(high50, "High-rate clusters, max 50%") +
  ss_map(low25, "Low-rate clusters, max 25%",
         colours = c("#08306B", "#2171B5", "#6BAED6", "#C6DBEF"))

# counties in the 50% most likely high-rate cluster that also sit in a
# significant low-rate cluster
in_mlc <- trimws(as.character(high50$gis$LOC_ID[high50$gis$CLUSTER == 1]))
in_low <- trimws(as.character(low25$gis$LOC_ID[low25$gis$P_VALUE < 0.05]))

pa_covid |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(GEOID %in% intersect(in_mlc, in_low)) |>
  select(NAME, deaths_2020, E, SMR)
```

**E1.** Where is the most likely **low-rate** cluster? Our expected deaths use
one statewide rate, with no adjustment for age. Give one reason other than
"less COVID-19" why a county or group of counties could have fewer deaths than
expected.

**The most likely low-rate cluster is Allegheny, Fayette, Greene, Washington. Pittsburgh is in Allegheny and a larger city in Pennsylvania, and is more likely to be more prepared and have more resources to prevent deaths from COVID-19 than a rural area. It's also possible they had better lockdown policies or restrictions in place to prevent the spread of COVID-19 more.**


**E2.** Does any county belong both to the most likely high-rate cluster at
50% and to a significant low-rate cluster? What does that tell you about how
to read the **outline** of a large cluster?

**Wayne county belongs to both. SaTScan identifies clusters based on the combined risk of all counties within the circle, so some counties may have lower death rates even when the overall cluster has a higher rate.**

## Part F --- Reproducibility and AI use (1 point)

Each run left its parameter file (`.prm`) in your `satscan` folder, and
SaTScan repeats every setting in a *PARAMETER SETTINGS* section at the end of
each results file. The main ones for `high50`:

```{r}
#| label: parameters

keep <- grep(paste("Type of Analysis", "Probability Model", "Scan For Areas With",
                   "Maximum Spatial Cluster Size", "Window Shape", "P-Value Reporting",
                   "Number of Replications", "Criteria for Reporting", sep = "|"), txt)
cat(trimws(txt[keep]), sep = "\n")
```

**F1.** Name three settings that someone would need to reproduce your most
likely cluster exactly. Why is a script that writes these settings more
reliable than a description of what you clicked in the SaTScan window?

**To reproduce most likely cluster they would need type of analysis: purely spatial, probability model: Poisson, and scan for areas with: high rates. A script is more reliable than describing what was clicked in SaTScan because it records the exact settings used and allows someone to rerun the analysis without manually entering them**

**F2.** End your document with one sentence on whether and how you used AI
tools.

**In Part B, question 5, used ChatGPT to understand the code given to see what in it had the map only showing p-values < 0.05. I used ChatGPT for part D, questions 1 and 2 to understand LLR better and how SaTScan calculates p-values.**
